title: I’m surrounded by idiots!?
content:
Kaya was taking a peaking into this world of humans on her travels and was captivated by this tale for human offsprings.

Maybe Scar’s quote resonated and captured that specific, deeply frustrating feeling of being the only one in the room who actually sees the big picture while everyone else is just fumbling around.

Kaya did not hate people. Hating people required a level of emotional investment she simply couldn’t afford to waste. No, Kaya’s affliction was much heavier, much more exhausting: she was simply, undeniably, surrounded by idiots.

She stood in the pristine, limestone archives of the High Cartography Institute, adjusting her magnifying loupe over a massive maritime chart. Around her, senior cartographers fumbled with delicate parchment and leaked standard charcoal ink over the borders as if they were wearing winter mittens. Kaya was the sharpest mind in the sector, a woman who had braved social norms to master the invisible laws of geography, terrain, and the precise, mathematical ratios of her own secret, no-spill ink.

And yet, every single day, she had to watch people smudge the lines.

Her phone vibrated against the marble counter. A message from the border transit office.

> **TRANSIT COURIER REGISTRY:** *Application Denied. Reason: Invalid Sector Coordinates.*

> 

Kaya closed her eyes, the rustle of a hundred heavy parchment maps around the room suddenly sounding like a collective, mocking laugh.

She had spent six figures in local credits—essentially her entire savings from her last major expedition—to secure Sovereign Passports and premium airship transit tokens for her parents and siblings. She wanted them to see her world. She wanted them to stand in the grand archives and finally understand the magnitude of the charts she created.

All they had to do was fill out a single, standard form. The coordinates of her institute were plastered on the front page of every major civic directory. It was a five-second lookup. Instead, they had guessed. They had written down a completely different district, misspelling the sector name entirely.

*I am surrounded by idiots,* her mind whispered, the phrase striking like a clean, dull hammer.

It wasn’t anger; it was the suffocating, hollow realization that they didn’t even care enough to look. They were content to stay in their small, dusty village, blind to the wild tides of the world, entirely incurious about the girl who mapped the stars.

“Kaya? Are you listening to me?”

She opened her eyes. Standing across the plotting table was Julian, her partner. He was currently holding a beautifully cured leather scroll casing—one he had completely sliced open by using the wrong boundary blade. He looked at her with the wide, helpless eyes of a child who had just dropped a glass jar.

“I tried to trim the borders like you asked,” Julian mumbled, shifting his weight. “But it tore. You knew how I was with the delicate leather when you chose to partner with me. Why are you acting so cold about it now?”

Kaya stared at him. This was his favorite defensive shield. *You knew how I was.* A grown man whose entire strategy in a partnership was to weaponize his own incompetence so she would sigh, take the blades from his hands, and do the plotting for him. He didn’t want to learn; he wanted a caretaker to fix his mistakes.

“Clean it up, Julian,” she said, her voice terrifyingly quiet.

She walked out of the drafting hall, her boots clicking sharply against the stone floor. She needed air. She needed a break from the gravity of everyone else’s laziness.

But the world outside offered no sanctuary. She owned a small residential complex down the road, a property she managed completely on her own to secure her financial independence. Just this morning, her tenants had sent a formal grievance because the courtyard vines were “too difficult to prune.” They expected her—a woman mapping the uncharted territories of the empire—to come over with shears and trim their walkways because basic yard work felt like an impossible riddle to them.

She marched toward the Guild Director’s office to clear her head with raw geographical data. The Director, a man whose title vastly outpaced his intellect, looked up from his heavy mahogany desk.

“Ah, Kaya,” he smiled, a patronizing, slow expression. “I saw your petition for the Senior Research Track. Fascinating work on the deep-sea topography grids. Truly intelligent.”

“Thank you, Director. I assume the board approved the promotion?”

The Director chuckled, leaning back. “Oh, we can’t do that. You see, the Senior Track is a permanent guild line. We don’t expect highly intelligent, hyper-capable people like yourself to actually stay with a company like ours for the long haul. You’ll catch a bigger wind, find a grander expedition, and leave us. So, we’re keeping you right where you are.”

Kaya’s breath caught in her throat. The room felt suddenly devoid of oxygen. It was a gilded cage. She was being punished for her excellence, held back because she was too good at her job, while the mediocre pool around her floated effortlessly to the top.

Desperate for some semblance of grounding, Kaya took the evening transport to the coastal edge of the city to visit her Elder Guardians—the sweet, traditional couple she had adopted as her chosen family. They lived in a beautiful, secluded cottage on the rocky shore, safe from the chaotic politics of the inner city. She thought they, at least, would offer a sanctuary of love.

They sat on the porch, watching the waves crash against the jagged rocks below. Kaya tried to explain the suffocating weight of her week, the isolation of doing everything alone, the desire to find something bigger.

The matriarch adjusted her knitted shawl, her face full of gentle, smothering pity.

“Oh, my dear Kaya.

This is what happens when you try to brave the wild waters of the world. The modern era is full of chaos. If an alliance or a career doesn’t come directly from a secluded, traditional arrangement from the supreme force—if it isn’t brought to you safely by the community—it is bound to be corrupt. You must stay on the shore where it’s safe.“

Kaya looked out at the raging ocean. Her knuckles turned white against her teacup reminding of the “Pearls don’t lie on the seashore. If you want one, you must dive for it” she picked from human world. She wanted to respond but it would only make her only family-like visits sour. Maybe she is has had too much influence of this world, doubted Kaya for a minute.

They were well-meaning wardens, but wardens nonetheless. They sat comfortably on the dry sand, never once dipping their toes into the freezing, violent depths, completely unaware that you have to actually survive the terrifying heights of the water if you ever want to reach down and grasp the pearl. They wanted her small as she was growing up. They wanted her compliant, which gave them pride to call her their own. Did they wanted her to mistake safety for peace?

The phrase returned, louder this time, a steady, rhythmic pulse in her temples.

I am surrounded by idiots.

The weight of their collective inadequacy pressed down on her chest like a concrete block. She was the one paying the credits, she was the one pulling the late nights, she was the one whose precise lines kept the trade ships from crashing into reefs—and yet she was entirely, profoundly alone in the dark.

Kaya stood up, setting her teacup down with a sharp clink. She looked at the gentle, smiling faces of her guardians, then turned her gaze back toward the glittering, chaotic lights of the city.

The realization had fully set in, crushing and absolute.

No one was coming to save her.

No one was going to help her pull the weight.

Fine ! If she had to carry the world on her back, she would do it.

But she was done pretending the anchors around her ankles were family.
